skill.name: Sentence openers that put the message up front
skill.why: The opener is where the reader starts. Choose it on purpose.
skill.how: Ask what the reader needs first. Put that at the start of the sentence.

options.reason: Like the opener there now, this says when, but a reader still has to guess the time of year.
Autumn already has its sentence, about fattening up. The long sleep comes after it.
This tells where. A reader planning a trip is looking for the time of year.

encounters.frame: Mo is writing his recipe for gum-leaf pancakes. The Frontnip is hoping for a taste.
encounters.text: Cooks glance at the clock first and the card second, so every step on Mo's card leads with the timing. Last time, Gus guessed when a pancake 'looked ready' and flipped it into the ceiling fan.
encounters.prompt: Build the next step so a cook who glances up knows exactly when to flip.
encounters.success: 'After ten minutes' leads with a time a cook can check. 'Looks ready' is timing too, but it's a guess.

tiles: After ten minutes in the pan,
accept: After ten minutes in the pan, flip each gum-leaf pancake with a wide spatula.
body.reason: Two tiles say when. Which one could a cook check on the clock?

encounters.frame: The editor of the Peaks Post is training new reporters. The Frontnip is on the desk, eating a pencil.
encounters.text: Ms Petrakis, the editor of the Peaks Post, tells every new reporter the same thing: the first words of a news story must deliver the news itself, not the weather, the scenery or the build-up. She has pinned these opening lines to the wall to show the difference.
encounters.prompt: Match each opening line to whether it puts the news first or makes the reader wait.
encounters.success: News-first openings tell you what happened straight away. The others make you wade through the build-up.

items.text: A runaway robot vacuum has eaten the mayor's hat, two cupcakes and a microphone at the opening of the new chairlift.
items.reason: The news, a robot vacuum eating the mayor's hat, comes in the very first words.

items.text: Snow has closed every ladder on the eastern towers, rangers announced this morning.
items.reason: The news, the ladders being closed, comes first. Who announced it comes after.

items.text: On a quiet Tuesday, as the sun rose over the valley and the kettles boiled, a wombat broke into the bakery.
items.reason: You read about Tuesday, sunrise and kettles before you reach the news about the wombat.

items.text: A local Year 6 student has built a slime that glows brighter than a torch.
items.reason: The news, a slime that glows, is in the first few words.

items.text: After weeks of rumours, careful planning and a lot of arguing in the town hall, the chairlift will finally reopen.
items.reason: You read about rumours and arguing first. The news, the chairlift reopening, is at the end.

items.text: The Peaks Under-12s have won the snow footy final by two points.
items.reason: The news, the team winning the final, is the first thing you read.

encounters.frame: Zed is writing a walkthrough for the Ice Palace level. The Frontnip is stuck somewhere inside.
encounters.text: The Ice Palace is the hardest level in Frostbite Quest, and Zed has finally written a walkthrough for it. Zed wrote it for players who get stuck halfway. The palace has four rooms, which players must clear in this order: the Great Hall, the Kitchen, the Library and the Throne Room. Each room has one big danger. In the Great Hall, a swarm of angry ice bats swoops from the ceiling, so keep moving and never stand still under the chandelier. In the Kitchen, the frozen chef throws icicles shaped like fish fingers, which you can dodge by ducking behind the giant fridge. In the Library, every book is a trap, apart from the blue one on the bottom shelf, which opens a secret door to the final room. ___, the Ice Queen waits on a throne of frozen custard, and she can only be defeated by a well-aimed snowball to the crown. Zed says the custard throne is the most disgusting thing he has ever seen in a game, and he has played Sewer Slugs 3.
encounters.prompt: Stuck players scan the walkthrough for the room they're in. Which opener fits the gap?
encounters.success: 'In the Throne Room' names the room up front, so a player stuck there finds their place at a glance.

options.reason: The Great Hall is the first room, with the ice bats. The Queen is in the last room.
This tells when, not where. A stuck player scanning for their room would skip right past it.
It tells how you got there, but names no room. A stuck player scans for room names.
